job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup we want to send Senator Whitfield's office a list of fixes. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let mining companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Based on the supplied text, these are the drafting issues I would flag for the October 15 markup. Some are clear exceptions; others create uncertainty rather than guaranteed defenses.

### Definitions and coverage

1. **Section 2(1)(A)—Per-vessel threshold permits fleet splitting.** The definition counts recovery by a “single vessel,” not by an operator, affiliated companies, project, or mining site. A company could distribute extraction among multiple vessels, each below the threshold, unless the Secretary separately brings the activity within section 2(1)(B).

2. **Section 2(1)(A)—Subthreshold mining remains permissible.** “More than 10,000 metric tons” excludes recovery of exactly 10,000 tons or less per vessel per year, regardless of its commercial purpose or cumulative ecological effects. The bill therefore establishes an extraction allowance rather than an unconditional commercial-mining prohibition, subject to the discretionary catchall.

3. **Section 2(1)(A)—The annual accounting period is undefined.** “Per year” could mean calendar year, operating year, or a rolling 12-month period. The text also leaves unclear whether planned recovery above the threshold is prohibited from the outset or whether liability begins only when actual recovery crosses it.

4. **Section 2(1)(A)—Tonnage measurement is unspecified.** The bill does not say whether to weigh wet material, dry material, ore, recovered minerals, or material before processing. Nor does it establish measurement methods or address discarded material, creating opportunities to undercount recovery.

5. **Section 2(1)(A)—The depth boundary is incomplete.** Recovery at exactly 200 meters is excluded, and the bill provides no depth-measurement standard or rule for operations spanning the boundary. It also does not clearly address extraction from beneath the seabed, rather than “from the seabed.”

6. **Section 2(1)(A)—Recovery “by a single vessel” leaves non-vessel systems uncertain.** Extraction using fixed platforms, seabed installations, autonomous equipment, or distributed collection-and-transfer systems may not fit the definition cleanly. The bill needs a rule attributing recovery to the operation regardless of the equipment configuration.

7. **Section 2(1)(A)—“Recovery” leaves mining stages uncovered.** Prospecting, exploration, seabed excavation without collection, equipment deployment, processing, and waste discharge are not expressly prohibited. Companies could continue damaging preparatory or associated operations that do not themselves constitute recovery, unless covered by a section 2(1)(B) determination.

8. **Section 2(1)—The title and operative definition do not match.** Despite the word “commercial,” the definition contains no sale, profit, or commercial-purpose requirement and could reach large scientific collections while excluding smaller profit-making operations. The bill should state whether purpose matters and define any legitimate research allowance separately.

9. **Section 2(1)(A)—“Other mineral resources” has uncertain boundaries.** The text does not specify whether the term includes sand and gravel, mineral-bearing sediments, dissolved minerals, or hydrocarbons. That uncertainty invites coverage disputes and potentially unintended application beyond the mining activities Congress means to prohibit.

10. **Section 2(1)(B)—“The Secretary” is undefined.** The bill never identifies the official authorized to designate additional prohibited activities. Section 6 names the Secretary of State and section 4 names NOAA, but neither resolves who administers this catchall.

11. **Section 2(1)(B)—The risk-comparison standard is indeterminate.** “Comparable” risks to “deep-sea ecosystems” lack defined measures of severity, probability, duration, geographic extent, or cumulative impact. Because the benchmark encompasses widely varying activities, the provision invites inconsistent decisions and fair-notice challenges, especially when used to support criminal liability.

12. **Section 2(1)(B)—The catchall has no required implementation process.** There is no deadline, required review of subthreshold activities, or procedure for making and publishing determinations. The bill also fails to specify when determinations become binding, leaving coverage dependent on agency initiative and creating uncertainty about notice and prospective enforcement.

13. **Section 2(2)—The entity definition is too narrow.** “Corporation organized under the laws of a State” does not expressly include LLCs, partnerships, trusts, unincorporated associations, or entities organized under federal, District of Columbia, territorial, or tribal law. These entities could argue that their overseas activities fall outside the prohibition.

14. **Section 2(2)—Foreign affiliates are not covered by ownership or control.** A foreign-incorporated subsidiary does not become a “U.S. person” merely because a U.S. company owns or controls it. The bill lacks an express anti-evasion rule addressing offshore affiliates, although a U.S. parent’s own conduct could still create liability depending on its involvement.

15. **Section 2(2)—Some U.S.-connected individuals are omitted.** The definition includes citizens but not noncitizen U.S. nationals or lawful permanent residents. Their conduct outside the United States is therefore not expressly covered merely because of those connections.

### Prohibition and exceptions

16. **Section 3(a)—The geographic scope of “in the United States” is undefined.** The bill does not specify treatment of territories, territorial waters, the exclusive economic zone, or the outer continental shelf. The latter two are not simply equivalent to U.S. territory, leaving uncertainty about foreign operators mining areas subject to U.S. resource jurisdiction.

17. **Sections 2(2) and 3(a)—U.S.-flagged vessels are not an independent jurisdictional basis.** A foreign person mining outside the United States aboard a U.S.-flagged vessel is not expressly covered on that basis alone. Vessel registration under section 4 does not itself extend section 3’s prohibition.

18. **Section 3(a)—“Engage in” does not allocate responsibility clearly.** The bill does not expressly identify owners, operators, charterers, controllers, contractors, or persons directing extraction as responsible parties. That leaves room to separate ownership, management, and physical operations among entities and dispute which ones committed a violation.

19. **Section 3(a)—Support activities and mineral trade are not expressly prohibited.** Financing, insuring, supplying, transporting, purchasing, importing, or selling deep-seabed minerals are not independently barred. General criminal complicity rules may reach some intentional assistance to an underlying crime, but they do not create a comprehensive civil prohibition or prevent support for foreign mining outside section 3’s reach.

20. **Section 3(b)—An exploration license becomes an exemption for mining.** The operative language exempts “mining conducted under an exploration license” without expressly limiting the exemption to lawful exploration activities or excluding commercial extraction. Even if existing licensing law supplies limits, this wording invites arguments that an exploration authorization protects continued mining from the new prohibition.

21. **Section 3(b)—Qualifying licenses are not identified.** The bill does not specify the issuing government or authority, governing statute, or requirement that a license remain valid and in good standing. Companies could argue that foreign or international authorizations qualify, or dispute whether expired, suspended, or otherwise defective licenses retain protection.

22. **Section 3(b)—Grandfathering has no scope or duration controls.** The exemption contains no express limits on renewal, extension, amendment, transfer, increased production, additional vessels, or expansion of the licensed area. It could consequently protect expanded or successor operations rather than merely winding down genuinely existing activity.

23. **Section 3(b)—Pre-enactment licensing creates a rush-to-qualify incentive.** Eligibility depends on license issuance, not whether operations had actually begun or substantial commitments had been made. A company could obtain a license shortly before enactment to claim protection, and the text does not address pending applications or backdated authorizations.

24. **Section 3(c)—Environmental assessment is an unrestricted purpose-based exception.** There is no requirement that assessment be the sole or primary purpose, so a commercially productive operation could assert an additional assessment purpose. The exemption has no extraction cap, duration limit, geographic limit, or restriction on selling recovered minerals.

25. **Section 3(c)—No approval or verification safeguards govern assessments.** The bill requires no advance authorization, independent scientific review, necessity finding, low-impact methods, monitoring, or publication of results. It also does not expressly exclude otherwise prohibited activities designated under section 2(1)(B), potentially allowing the exception to defeat that catchall.

26. **Sections 3(b)–(c)—Exemptions are difficult to verify.** Operators need not notify an agency that they claim an exemption, retain supporting records, or submit evidence of eligibility. The bill also leaves the allocation of proof unstated, increasing enforcement disputes over licenses and asserted assessment purposes.

27. **Section 3 and the bill generally—Interaction with existing legal authority is unresolved.** The bill does not expressly coordinate the prohibition with the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act or other relevant leasing and permitting regimes, or direct agencies to stop issuing conflicting authorizations. An existing permit would not necessarily override a later prohibition, but leaving the overlap unresolved invites litigation and inconsistent administration.

### Registry and reporting

28. **Sections 2(3) and 4(a)—Registry coverage does not match prohibited conduct.** Vessels of 5,000 gross tons or less, fixed installations, and potentially vessels supporting activities designated under section 2(1)(B) escape registration. This is a monitoring gap, not an exemption from section 3: a smaller vessel can still conduct prohibited mining.

29. **Section 2(3)—Vessel size and equipment standards are unclear.** The bill specifies neither the gross-tonnage measurement convention nor when a vessel counts as “equipped” for recovery. Modular equipment, temporary removal, and reliance on separate seabed machinery could generate registration disputes.

30. **Section 4(a)—The registration obligation has no jurisdictional limit.** “Each covered vessel” appears to reach vessels worldwide without regard to flag, ownership, location, or U.S. contacts. That creates practical enforcement problems and invites jurisdictional challenges or a narrowing construction.

31. **Section 4(a)—Registration timing and responsibility are unspecified.** There is no deadline, requirement to register before operations, definition of “operator,” or process for ownership and operational changes. Multiple parties could dispute responsibility while a vessel continues operating.

32. **Section 4(b)—Only registered operators must report.** An operator that fails to register can argue that the separate reporting duty never attached. Reporting should attach to everyone required to register, regardless of actual compliance.

33. **Section 4(b)—Required reports lack essential content and deadlines.** “Describing” recovery activities does not expressly require quantities, coordinates, depths, dates, mineral types, vessel identifiers, or claimed exemptions. “Quarterly” also lacks a filing deadline, and the reports need not cover damaging activities that do not involve recovery.

34. **Sections 4 and 5—Registry and reporting violations lack express penalties.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of section 3, not failures to register, report, certify accurately, or maintain records. General false-statement law may apply to some knowing misrepresentations, but it does not supply a complete enforcement regime for section 4.

### Administration and penalties

35. **Sections 3–5—No lead enforcement agency or adequate investigative authority is designated.** NOAA receives registrations and reports, but the bill does not expressly assign enforcement responsibility or grant inspection, vessel-tracking, sampling, audit, subpoena, or recordkeeping authority. Existing authority may cover some situations, but the bill leaves major evidentiary and interagency gaps.

36. **Section 5(a)—The civil-penalty process is missing.** The bill does not specify whether penalties are assessed administratively or sought in court, who brings the case, or the procedures for notice, hearings, collection, and review. This omission complicates implementation and risks procedural challenges.

37. **Section 5(a)—Daily violations are not defined.** It is unclear how an annual recovery threshold translates into particular days of violation, including whether earlier extraction days count once the threshold is crossed. The text also leaves uncertain whether multiple vessels or projects generate separate penalties on the same day.

38. **Section 5(a)—Penalty calibration may leave profitable violations.** The bill provides only a maximum, with no express factors tied to economic benefit, ecological harm, repetition, or ability to pay. It also provides no explicit recovery of unlawful profits, so penalties below the maximum could become a business expense.

39. **Section 5(b)—“Willfully” is undefined.** Its interpretation could materially affect whether prosecutors must prove awareness of unlawfulness or some more specific knowledge. The combination of this uncertainty, technical thresholds, discretionary designations, and broad exceptions makes criminal cases harder to establish.

40. **Sections 3–5—Preventive and remedial enforcement tools are not expressly provided.** The bill lacks explicit stop-work orders, vessel detention or forfeiture, injunctive authority, and liability for restoration or assessment costs. Other law may supply some remedies, but fines and imprisonment alone do not ensure rapid cessation or repair of damage.

41. **Sections 3–5—No supplemental enforcement safeguards are included.** There is no citizen-suit mechanism or mining-specific whistleblower protection, and no express public-access requirement for registry and reporting data. Enforcement therefore depends heavily on government initiative and on evidence controlled by operators.

### International agreement, duration, and effective date

42. **Section 6—The diplomatic deadline does not require a result.** “Seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months” is unclear about whether negotiations must begin or an agreement must be secured by then. It requires neither a binding agreement nor specified participation, compliance mechanisms, interim milestones, or progress reports.

43. **Section 6—“Equivalent” prohibitions could export the domestic exceptions.** Referencing section 3 incorporates a provision containing broad licensing and assessment carveouts. The bill does not clearly instruct negotiators to obtain a comprehensive prohibition rather than an international arrangement reproducing those weaknesses.

44. **Section 7(a)—The scientific off-ramp lacks a defined standard and process.** “Without serious harm” does not identify acceptable risk, cumulative effects, geographic scale, evidentiary confidence, or the duration of assessment. No one is required to commission or fund the National Academies report, and the text does not specify its scope, independence safeguards, or treatment of uncertainty.

45. **Section 7(a)—A narrow finding could lift the entire prohibition.** The provision does not require a finding that all otherwise prohibited forms of mining can be conducted safely. Evidence about one technology, mineral, or location could be invoked to terminate section 3 wholesale rather than authorize only that limited activity.

46. **Sections 7(a)–(b)—The ten-year sunset overrides the apparent safety condition.** The entire Act expires after ten years even if Congress has made no safety finding and the scientific evidence still shows serious risks. Registry, reporting, and other statutory provisions also expire, so this is not a durable prohibition pending proof of safety.

47. **Section 7—Termination and transition rules are incomplete.** The text does not clearly specify what happens to implementing determinations, records, pending proceedings, or continuing obligations when the prohibition or Act ends. General federal savings law may preserve certain accrued liabilities, but express transition language would avoid disputes about its reach.

48. **Sections 5(a) and 8—Civil liability and the effective date conflict.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, while section 8 delays the Act’s effectiveness by 180 days. That creates uncertainty over whether early conduct is lawful or subject to later civil penalties and should be resolved with one clear liability start date.

49. **Section 8—The delayed effective date permits an operational grace period.** On the natural reading of section 8, otherwise lawful mining can continue for 180 days after enactment before the prohibition applies. There is no interim stop-work provision or requirement that registration and monitoring begin earlier.
